column4: The source-section gloss says a good name spreads in goodness, not evil; this verse forbids insulting epithets and calls the post-faith name of wrongdoing an evil name, بِئْسَ الِاسْمُ الْفُسُوقُ.
The source-section dictionary describes a rider with a mark in battle; here the angelic reinforcements are marked, مُسَوِّمِينَ, in a battle scene.
The source-section defines a sign as a mark by which something is known; the chest bearing relics is called آيَةَ مُلْكِهِ, the identifying sign of Saul's kingship.
The source-section dictionary form أَثَر is a trace one reads; Moses and his companion follow their آثار to find the place they sought.
The source section treats a trace as evidence; Joseph's brothers bring a shirt with false blood, بِدَمٍ كَذِبٍ, so the stain is a fabricated mark rather than a reliable sign.
The source-section's trace-reading image meets the test of Joseph's torn shirt: its tear from behind, قُدَّ مِن دُبُرٍ, is the distinguishing evidence.
This verse applies the garment test: seeing the tear from behind exposes the false accusation, so a physical trace separates truth from falsehood.
The source-section explains ع ل م through a sign that enables knowing; this verse calls the revelation clear signs, آيَاتٌ بَيِّنَاتٌ, in the breasts of those given عِلْم.
The section says created things are signs that disclose what they are not; after describing creation, this verse distinguishes the Creator from what does not create.
The section's ruined town is read as a sign; this verse says a clear sign, آيَةً بَيِّنَةً, was left from the town of Lot.
The source section connects traces of a ruined town with discerning its lesson; this verse says a sign was left there for those who fear punishment.
The source image is a mark by which a person is recognized; this verse says bliss is recognizable in their faces, نَضْرَةَ النَّعِيمِ.
The section's root ع ل م links signs to knowing and mentions traces; this verse challenges claims for other gods with a demand for creation, authority, scripture, or أَثَارَةٍ مِنْ عِلْمٍ.
The source-section describes a good name as raised mention; this verse commands, وَاذْكُرْ فِي الْكِتَابِ إِدْرِيسَ, to mention Idris in the Book.
The section's marks identify people on the heights; this continuation has those on al-A'raf call men they recognize by their marks, يَعْرِفُونَهُم بِسِيمَاهُمْ.
The source-section treats a mark as identifying an animal's status; this verse forbids violating God's rites and specifically names offerings and garlands as a protected boundary.
The section names the ark's motion and mooring; after it sails in 11:41-42, this verse records it coming to rest on Judi, completing the stopping detail.
This continuation interprets Noah's ark story from 23:27-29 as containing signs, إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَاتٍ, linking the vessel scene to the section's world-as-sign image.
This ayah supplies the ark antecedent for the section's later sign: Noah is carried in a vessel of planks and nails before 54:15 says it was left as a sign.
This continuation says the ark sails under God's watch; 54:15 then names the surviving vessel as a sign, adding divine care to the marked scene.
The source-section's branded camel is an animal marked for recognition; this verse groups sacrificial offerings with garlands, الْهَدْيَ وَالْقَلَائِدَ, as public institutions for people.
The source section connects God's name with worship; between the rite in 22:34 and the named offerings in 22:36, this verse describes hearts trembling when Allah is mentioned.
The source section's brand at 68:16 marks a rejecter; this immediate predecessor says he calls God's verses tales of the ancients, supplying the rejection the mark follows.
The section's image makes a mark identify its bearer; after 55:41 identifies criminals by their marks, this verse identifies the destination as Hell.
The section names the ark's motion and stopping; after 42:32 calls sailing ships signs like standards, this verse says God's wind can hold them still.
This continuation extends the ship sign in 36:41 to other vessels people ride, broadening the reader's view from Noah's ark to conveyances.
The source-section links the name to height; after 19:56 tells readers to mention Idris in the Book, this verse says God raised him to a high station.
The source section places the separate roots س م و (height) and ع ل م (knowing) together; this verse raises people given عِلْم in degrees, though عِلْم here means knowledge, not a sign.
The source section defines an identifying sign; this verse says the Sacred House contains clear signs, including the standing place of Abraham, مَقَامُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ.
This verse supplies two concrete idol names, al-Lat and al-Uzza; the passage's later critique at 53:23 says such names were assigned by people without authority.
This verse adds Manat to the named idols; the passage's critique at 53:23 supplies the point that these are human-given names without authority.
This continuation calls the angelic support glad tidings and reassurance; it explains how the marked battle scene in 3:125 functions as a sign.
The section says a mark distinguishes its bearer; this verse contrasts faces that turn white and faces that turn black on the Day of Judgment.
This continuation gives the white-faced group its identity: they are in Allah's mercy and remain there.
The section's mark makes a person recognizable; this verse presents radiant faces as a visible sign of their state.
This continuation completes the radiant faces with their smiling and rejoicing, making their condition legible.
This verse reverses the radiant-face scene with faces carrying dust, a visible mark of the other group.
This continuation adds darkness covering the dusty faces, completing the contrary visible sign.
This verse identifies the people bearing the dark facial signs as disbelievers and wicked, completing what the marks disclose.
The source-section trace is something seen and read; Joseph's shirt is torn from behind, a physical clue whose meaning the following verses test.
This continuation introduces a witness's front-versus-back test for the torn shirt; its contribution is the competing accounts that make the trace decisive.
The section's dictionary gloss describes recognizing a trace in someone; Jacob says he senses Yusuf's scent, رِيحَ يُوسُفَ, as an identifying trace before the caravan arrives.
The source-section says an act begun under a name is placed under its bearer; this declaration dedicates prayer, sacrifice, life, and death to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
The section defines a name as what identifies its bearer; this verse calls each people with its imam, بِإِمَامِهِم, an indirect identifying affiliation rather than a literal name.
The source-section dictionary form أَثَر is a trace; this verse speaks of a people following their fathers' آثار, an indirect inherited-tradition parallel rather than a literal brand.
The verse calls the drink رَحِيقٍ مَخْتُومٍ, matching the section's brand as a mark; 83:26 says its seal/finish is musk, though خِتَام may refer to its final taste rather than a physical seal.
